claims.text: The relevant starting material is an equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloy.
The proposed intervention is to add a small amount of Ti to CoCrFeNi.
The intervention is applicable at room temperature and normal pressure.
Adding Ti to CoCrFeNi forms a hard secondary phase.
The hard secondary phase produces precipitation strengthening.
Ti addition increases the strength of CoCrFeNi relative to the alloy without Ti.
Ti addition increases the hardness of CoCrFeNi relative to the alloy without Ti.
The Ti-modified alloy retains the favorable mechanical characteristics of the unmodified alloy.
The comparison baseline is CoCrFeNi without Ti.
The applicable Ti-content range is 0 to 1.5 in the CoCrFeNiTix molar-ratio notation.
The effects of Ti content on microstructure and mechanical properties remain uncertain.
The hypothesis can be tested by preparing alloys with varying Ti content and measuring tensile strength, hardness, and microstructure.
Failure of Ti addition to improve both strength and hardness relative to CoCrFeNi would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The stated starting material already contains approximately equimolar Ti, but the intervention is framed as adding Ti to a Ti-free CoCrFeNi baseline. Thus the intervention does not operate on the stated starting state.
The intervention calls the Ti addition small, whereas the upper bound x = 1.5 corresponds to about 27.3 at.% Ti in CoCrFeNiTi1.5, which is not clearly a small addition.

The proposed mediator is a hard secondary phase, but the cited CoCrFeNiTix processing study reports a single-phase FCC structure throughout x = 0–1.5. The other cited record supports secondary-phase formation only as a general literature statement and does not resolve this processing-dependent inconsistency.
